danish.title: Tredje bog (1805) — Kapitel 5
paragraphs: De skiltes alle, men bortset fra Anatole, der faldt i søvn, så snart han lagde sig, lå alle længe vågne den nat.

»Skal han virkelig være min ægtemand, denne fremmede, som er så venlig — ja, venlig, det er det vigtigste,« tænkte fyrstinde Marja; og en frygt, hun sjældent havde oplevet, greb hende. Hun var bange for at se sig om; det syntes hende, at nogen stod bag skærmbræt i det mørke hjørne. Og denne nogen var ham — djævelen — og han var også denne mand med den hvide pande, de sorte bryn og de røde læber.
Hun ringede på sin kammerpige og bad hende sove i sit værelse.

Frøken Bourienne gik i lang tid op og ned i drivhuset den aften, forgæves ventende på nogen, snart smilende til nogen, snart arbejdende sig op til tårer over de indbildte ord fra sin pauvre mère, der bebrejdede hende hendes fald.

Den lille fyrstinde klagede til sin kammerpige over, at sengen var dårligt redt. Hun kunne hverken ligge på maven eller på siden. Enhver stilling var ubekvem og besværlig, og hendes byrde trykkede hende nu mere end nogen sinde, fordi Anatoles nærhed så levende havde mindet hende om den tid, da hun ikke var sådan, og alt var let og muntert. Hun sad i en lænestol i sin nattrøje og natkappe, og Katie, søvnig og uredt, bankede og vendte den tunge dundyne for tredje gang, mens hun mumlede for sig selv.

»Jeg sagde jo, at det hele var knuder og huller!« gentog den lille fyrstinde. »Jeg ville jo gerne falde i søvn, så det er ikke min skyld!« og hendes stemme skælvede som et barns, der er lige ved at græde.

Den gamle fyrste sov heller ikke. Tikhon, halvt i søvne, hørte ham trampe vredt rundt og fnøse. Den gamle fyrste følte sig, som om han var blevet fornærmet gennem sin datter. Fornærmelsen var desto mere sårende, fordi den ikke gjaldt ham selv, men en anden — hans datter, som han elskede højere end sig selv. Han blev ved med at sige til sig selv, at han ville overveje hele sagen og afgøre, hvad der var rigtigt, og hvad han burde gøre, men i stedet ophidsede han sig bare mere og mere.

»Den første den bedste — og hun glemmer sin far og alt andet, løber ovenpå og sætter sit hår op og logrer med halen og er sig selv ulig! Glad for at kaste sin far over bord! Og hun vidste, jeg ville lægge mærke til det. Fr... fr... fr! Og kan jeg ikke se, at den idiot kun havde øjne for Bourienne — hende må jeg skille mig af med. Og hvordan kan hun ikke have stolthed nok til at se det? Har hun ingen stolthed for sin egen skyld, så måtte hun dog have nogen for min! Jeg skal nok vise hende, at den døgenigt ikke tænker et sekund på hende og kun kigger på Bourienne. Nej, hun har ingen stolthed... men det skal jeg nok lære hende...«

Den gamle fyrste vidste, at hvis han fortalte datteren, at hun tog fejl, og at Anatole havde til hensigt at flirte med frøken Bourienne, ville fyrstinde Marjas selvfølelse blive såret, og hans eget mål (ikke at blive skilt fra hende) ville være nået — og beroliget af denne tanke kaldte han Tikhon og begyndte at klæde sig af.

»Hvilken djævel bragte dem hertil?« tænkte han, mens Tikhon trak natskjorten over hans udtørrede, gamle krop og gråhårede bryst. »Jeg inviterede dem aldrig. De kom for at forstyrre mit liv — og der er ikke meget af det tilbage.«
»Fanden tage dem!« mumlede han, mens hans hoved endnu var dækket af skjorten.
Tikhon kendte sin herres vane med undertiden at tænke højt og mødte derfor med uforandret mine det vredt spørgende udtryk i det ansigt, der dukkede frem fra skjorten.
»Er de gået i seng?« spurgte fyrsten.
Tikhon, der som alle gode kammerherrer instinktivt forstod sin herres tankegang, gættede, at spørgsmålet gjaldt fyrst Vasilij og hans søn.
»De er gået i seng og har slukket lyset, Deres excellence.«
»Det duer ikke... det duer ikke...« sagde fyrsten hurtigt, og idet han stak fødderne i tøflerne og armene i slabrockens ærmer, gik hen til den sofa, han sov på.

Skønt der ikke var faldet et ord mellem Anatole og frøken Bourienne, forstod de hinanden fuldkomment med hensyn til den første del af deres roman — op til det øjeblik, hvor la pauvre mère skulle vise sig; de forstod, at de havde meget at sige hinanden under fire øjne, og havde derfor siden morgenstunden søgt en lejlighed til at mødes alene. Da fyrstinde Marja gik ind til sin far på den sædvanlige tid, mødtes frøken Bourienne og Anatole i drivhuset.

Fyrstinde Marja gik til studerekammerdørens med en særlig bæven. Det syntes hende, at ikke blot alle vidste, at hendes skæbne ville blive afgjort den dag, men at de også vidste, hvad hun tænkte om det. Hun læste det i Tikhons ansigt og i fyrst Vasilijs kammertjeners, der bukkede dybt, da han mødte hende i gangen med varmt vand.

Den gamle fyrste var meget kærlig og omhyggelig i sin behandling af datteren den morgen. Fyrstinde Marja kendte godt dette omhyggelige udtryk hos sin far. Hans ansigt bar det udtryk, når hans tørre hænder knyttede sig i irritation over, at hun ikke forstod et regnestykke, når han rejste sig fra stolen og gik bort fra hende, mens han med dæmpet stemme gentog de samme ord adskillige gange.
Han kom straks til sagen og behandlede hende ceremonielt.

»Jeg har fået et forslag angående dig,« sagde han med et unaturligt smil. »Du har vel gættet, at fyrst Vasilij ikke er kommet og har medbragt sin elev« (af en eller anden grund kaldte fyrst Bolkonskij Anatole en »elev«) »for mine smukke øjnes skyld. I går aftes blev der fremsat et forslag til mig angående dig, og da du kender mine principper, overlader jeg det til dig.«
»Hvordan skal jeg forstå Dem, mon père?« sagde fyrstinden og blev bleg og derefter rød.
»Forstå mig!« råbte faderen vredt. »Fyrst Vasilij finder dig efter sin smag som svigerdatter og fremsætter et forslag på sin elevs vegne. Sådan skal det forstås! 'Forstå det'!... Og jeg spørger dig!«
»Jeg ved ikke, hvad De mener, far,« hviskede fyrstinden.
»Jeg? Jeg? Hvad med mig? Lad mig være udenfor. Jeg skal ikke giftes. Hvad med dig? Det er, hvad jeg vil vide.«

Fyrstinden indså, at faderen betragtede sagen med mishag, men i det øjeblik slog det hende, at hendes skæbne nu eller aldrig ville blive afgjort. Hun slog øjnene ned for ikke at se det blik, under hvilket hun følte, at hun ikke kunne tænke, men kun af vane underkaste sig, og sagde: »Jeg ønsker kun at gøre Deres vilje, men hvis jeg skulle udtrykke mit eget ønske...« Hun nåede ikke at sige det færdigt. Den gamle fyrste afbrød hende.
»Udmærket!« råbte han. »Han tager dig med din medgift og tager frøken Bourienne med i købet. Hun bliver konen, mens du...«
Fyrsten standsede. Han så den virkning, hans ord havde haft på datteren. Hun sænkede hovedet og var ved at briste i gråd.

»Nå, nå, det var bare for sjov!« sagde han. »Husk dette, fyrstinde: jeg holder fast ved det princip, at en pige har fuld ret til at vælge. Jeg giver dig friheden. Husk blot, at din lykke afhænger af din beslutning. Tænk ikke på mig!«
»Men det ved jeg ikke, far!«

»Det behøver du heller ikke sige noget om! Han får sine ordrer og gifter sig med dig eller hvem som helst; men du er fri til at vælge... Gå ind på dit værelse, tænk det over og kom igen om en time og sig mig i hans nærværelse: ja eller nej. Jeg ved, du vil bede over det. Nå, bed, hvis du vil, men det er bedre at tænke det over. Gå! Ja eller nej, ja eller nej, ja eller nej!« råbte han stadig, da fyrstinden, som i en tåge, allerede vaklende var gået ud af studereværelset.

Hendes skæbne var afgjort, og lykkeligt afgjort. Men hvad faderen havde sagt om frøken Bourienne var forfærdeligt. Det var usandt, selvfølgelig, men alligevel var det frygteligt, og hun kunne ikke lade være med at tænke på det. Hun gik lige igennem drivhuset, hverken seende eller hørende noget, da hun pludselig blev vækket af frøken Bouriennes velkendte hvisken. Hun løftede blikket, og to skridt borte så hun Anatole omfavne franskmanden og hviske noget til hende. Med et forfærdet udtryk i sit smukke ansigt så Anatole på fyrstinde Marja, men tog ikke straks armen fra frøken Bouriennes talje, som endnu ikke havde set hende.

»Hvem er det? Hvorfor? Vent et øjeblik!« syntes Anatoles ansigt at sige. Fyrstinde Marja så på dem i tavshed. Hun kunne ikke forstå det. Til sidst udstødte frøken Bourienne et skrig og løb bort. Anatole bukkede for fyrstinde Marja med et muntert smil, som om han indbød hende til at le med af dette mærkelige tilfælde, og idet han trak på skuldrene, gik han hen til den dør, der førte til hans egne værelser.

En time senere kom Tikhon for at kalde fyrstinde Marja til den gamle fyrste; han tilføjede, at fyrst Vasilij også var til stede. Da Tikhon kom til hende, sad fyrstinde Marja på sofaen i sit værelse og holdt den grædende frøken Bourienne i sine arme, mens hun blidt strøg hendes hår. Fyrstindens smukke øjne med al deres tidligere, rolige glans kiggede med øm hengivenhed og medlidenhed på frøken Bouriennes smukke ansigt.
»Nej, fyrstinde, jeg har for evigt mistet Deres hengivenhed!« sagde frøken Bourienne.
»Hvorfor? Jeg elsker Dem mere end nogen sinde,« sagde fyrstinde Marja, »og jeg vil forsøge at gøre alt, hvad jeg kan, for Deres lykke.«
»Men De foragter mig. De, som er så ren, kan aldrig forstå at blive revet med af lidenskab. Åh, bare min stakkels mor...«
»Jeg forstår det udmærket,« svarede fyrstinde Marja med et bedrøvet smil. »Rolig, min kære. Jeg går ind til min far,« sagde hun og gik ud.

Fyrst Vasilij, med det ene ben kastet højt over det andet og en snustobaksdåse i hånden, sad med et smil af dyb bevægelse i ansigtet, som om han var rørt til sit inderste og selv beklagede og lo af sin egen følsomhed, da fyrstinde Marja trådte ind. Han tog hastigt en pris tobak.

»Ah, min kære, min kære!« begyndte han, idet han rejste sig og tog begge hendes hænder. Så sukkede han og tilføjede: »Min søns skæbne er i Deres hænder. Beslut, min kære, gode, milde Marie, som jeg altid har elsket som en datter!«
Han trådte tilbage, og en virkelig tåre viste sig i hans øje.

»Fr... fr...« fnøs fyrst Bolkonskij. »Fyrsten gør dig et forslag på sin elevs — det vil sige, sin søns — vegne. Ønsker du eller ønsker du ikke at blive fyrst Anatole Kuragins hustru? Svar: ja eller nej!« råbte han. »Og derefter forbeholder jeg mig retten til også at udtale min mening. Ja, min mening, og kun min mening,« tilføjede fyrst Bolkonskij og vendte sig mod fyrst Vasilij som svar på dennes bønfaldende blik. »Ja eller nej?«
»Mit ønske er aldrig at forlade Dem, far, aldrig at adskille mit liv fra Deres. Jeg ønsker ikke at gifte mig,« svarede hun bestemt og kiggede med sine smukke øjne på fyrst Vasilij og sin far.

»Vrøvl! Nonsens! Vrøvl, vrøvl, vrøvl!« udbrød fyrst Bolkonskij med rynkede bryn og tog datterens hånd; han kyssede hende ikke, men bøjede kun sin pande mod hendes og pressede hendes hånd, så hun skar en grimasse og udstødte et lille skrig.
Fyrst Vasilij rejste sig.

»Min kære, jeg må sige Dem, at dette er et øjeblik, jeg aldrig, aldrig vil glemme. Men, min kære, vil De ikke give os et lille håb om at røre dette hjerte, så venligt og ædelmodigt? Sig 'måske'... Fremtiden er så lang. Sig 'måske.'«
»Fyrste, hvad jeg har sagt, er alt, hvad der er i mit hjerte. Jeg takker Dem for æren, men jeg vil aldrig blive Deres søns hustru.«

»Nå, så er det overstået, min kære! Jeg er meget glad for at have set Dem. Meget glad! Gå tilbage til dit værelse, fyrstinde. Gå!« sagde den gamle fyrste. »Meget, meget glad for at have set Dem,« gentog han og omfavnede fyrst Vasilij.

»Mit kald er et andet,« tænkte fyrstinde Marja. »Mit kald er at være lykkelig med en anden slags lykke — kærlighedens og selvopofringens lykke. Og koste hvad det vil, jeg vil arrangere stakkels Amélies lykke — hun elsker ham så lidenskabeligt og angrer så lidenskabeligt. Jeg vil gøre alt, hvad der står i min magt, for at arrangere et parti mellem dem. Hvis han ikke er rig, vil jeg give hende midlerne; jeg vil bede min far og Andrej. Jeg vil være så lykkelig, når hun er hans hustru. Hun er så ulykkelig, en fremmed, alene, hjælpeløs! Og, Å Gud, hvor lidenskabeligt hun må elske ham, siden hun kunne glemme sig selv sådan! Måske kunne jeg have gjort det samme!...« tænkte fyrstinde Marja.

english.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: They all went their separate ways, but except for Anatole, who fell asleep the moment he hit the pillow, everyone lay awake for a long time that night.

"Is he really going to be my husband, this stranger who is so kind — yes, kind, that's the most important thing," thought Princess Mary. Then a fear she rarely experienced came over her. She was afraid to look behind her — it felt as though someone was standing there behind the screen in the dark corner. And that someone was the devil — and he was also this man with the white forehead, black eyebrows, and red lips.
She rang for her maid and asked her to sleep in her room.

Mademoiselle Bourienne paced the conservatory for a long time that evening, waiting in vain for someone, alternately smiling at imaginary encounters and working herself up to tears with the imagined words of her poor mother scolding her for her moral downfall.

The little princess complained to her maid that the bed was badly made. She couldn't get comfortable lying on her stomach or on her side. Every position felt awkward and unbearable, and the weight of her pregnancy bothered her more than ever because Anatole's presence had vividly reminded her of the time when she wasn't like this, when everything was light and carefree. She sat in an armchair in her dressing jacket and nightcap while Katie, sleepy and disheveled, beat and turned the heavy feather mattress for the third time, muttering to herself.
"I told you it was all lumps and holes!" the little princess repeated. "I'd love to fall asleep — it's not my fault!" Her voice quivered like a child about to cry.

The old prince couldn't sleep either. Tikhon, half asleep, heard him pacing angrily and snorting. The old prince felt as if he'd been insulted through his daughter. The insult stung all the more because it wasn't directed at him personally, but at his daughter, whom he loved more than himself. He kept telling himself he would think the whole matter through carefully and decide what was right, but instead he only got more and more worked up.

"The first man who comes along — she forgets her father and everything else, runs upstairs and does her hair and wags her tail and becomes a different person! Happy to throw her father over! And she knew I'd notice. Hmph... hmph... hmph! And can't I see that idiot only had eyes for Bourienne — I'll have to get rid of her. And how is it she doesn't have enough pride to see it? If she has no pride for her own sake, she should at least have some for mine! She needs to be shown that this fool thinks nothing of her and only looks at Bourienne. No, she has no pride... but I'll show her..."

The old prince knew that if he told his daughter she was mistaken, that Anatole was really interested in Mademoiselle Bourienne, it would wound Princess Mary's self-esteem, and his own goal — not to be separated from her — would be achieved. Calming himself with this thought, he called Tikhon and began to undress.

"What the devil brought them here?" he thought, while Tikhon pulled the nightshirt over his dried-up old body and gray-haired chest. "I never invited them. They came to disrupt my life — and there isn't much of it left."
"Devil take them!" he muttered while his head was still covered by the shirt.
Tikhon knew his master's habit of sometimes thinking aloud, so he met the angry, questioning expression on the face that emerged from the shirt with an unchanged look.
"Have they gone to bed?" the prince asked.
Tikhon, like all good valets, instinctively sensed the direction of his master's thoughts. He guessed the question was about Prince Vasili and his son.
"They've retired and put out their lights, your excellency."
"No good... no good..." the prince said quickly, and thrusting his feet into his slippers and his arms into his dressing gown, he went to the couch where he slept.

Although no words had passed between Anatole and Mademoiselle Bourienne, they understood each other perfectly regarding the first act of their romance, up to the appearance of the poor mother. They understood they had much to say to each other in private and had been looking for a chance to meet alone since morning. When Princess Mary went to her father's room at the usual hour, Mademoiselle Bourienne and Anatole met in the conservatory.

Princess Mary approached the door of the study with particular dread. It seemed to her that not only did everyone know her fate would be decided that day, but that they also knew what she thought about it. She read this in Tikhon's face and in the face of Prince Vasili's valet, who gave her a deep bow when she passed him in the corridor carrying hot water.

The old prince was unusually gentle and attentive in his treatment of his daughter that morning. Princess Mary knew this painstaking manner well. His face wore that expression when his dry hands clenched in frustration at her not understanding an arithmetic problem, when he would get up from his chair and walk away, repeating the same words in a low voice several times.
He came straight to the point, treating her with a forced formality.

"I've received a proposal concerning you," he said with an unnatural smile. "I expect you've guessed that Prince Vasili didn't come here and bring his pupil" — for some reason Prince Bolkonsky referred to Anatole as a 'pupil' — "just to admire my beautiful eyes. Last night a proposal was made on your behalf, and as you know my principles, I'm leaving the decision to you."
"How should I understand you, Father?" said the princess, growing pale and then blushing.

"What do you mean, how?" her father cried angrily. "Prince Vasili has taken a liking to you as a daughter-in-law and is proposing on his pupil's behalf. That's what there is to understand! 'How should I understand?' ... I'm the one asking you!"
"I don't know what you think, Father," the princess whispered.
"Me? What about me? Leave me out of this. I'm not the one getting married. What about you? That's what I want to know."

The princess could see that her father disapproved, but at that moment the thought struck her that her fate would be decided now or never. She lowered her eyes to avoid his gaze, under which she felt she could only submit out of habit rather than think clearly, and said: "I only want to do your will, but if I had to express my own wish..." She didn't have time to finish. The old prince cut her off.
"Wonderful!" he shouted. "He'll take you with your dowry and grab Mademoiselle Bourienne as a bonus. She'll be the real wife, while you..."
The prince stopped. He saw the effect his words had on his daughter. She lowered her head and was about to burst into tears.

"Now then, now then — I'm only joking!" he said. "Remember this, Princess: I believe firmly that a young woman has every right to choose. I'm giving you complete freedom. Just remember that your life's happiness depends on your decision. Don't worry about me!"
"But I don't know, Father!"

"There's no need for discussion! He takes orders and will marry you or anyone else. But you are free to choose... Go to your room, think it over, and come back in an hour to tell me in his presence: yes or no. I know you'll pray about it. Fine, pray if you want, but you'd better think it over too. Go! Yes or no, yes or no, yes or no!" he kept shouting even as the princess, as if lost in a fog, had already stumbled out of the study.

Her fate was decided, and happily decided. But what her father had said about Mademoiselle Bourienne was terrible. It couldn't be true, of course, but still it was awful, and she couldn't stop thinking about it. She was walking straight through the conservatory, not seeing or hearing anything, when suddenly the familiar whispering of Mademoiselle Bourienne snapped her out of her daze. She looked up and, two steps away, saw Anatole with his arms around the Frenchwoman, whispering something to her. With a look of horror on his handsome face, Anatole glanced at Princess Mary but didn't immediately remove his arm from Mademoiselle Bourienne's waist — she hadn't yet noticed the princess.

"Who's that? Why? Wait a moment!" Anatole's face seemed to say. Princess Mary stared at them in silence. She couldn't make sense of it. Finally Mademoiselle Bourienne let out a scream and ran off. Anatole bowed to Princess Mary with a cheerful smile, as if inviting her to laugh at this strange scene, then shrugged his shoulders and walked toward the door leading to his own rooms.

An hour later, Tikhon came to summon Princess Mary to the old prince, adding that Prince Vasili was there too. When Tikhon arrived, Princess Mary was sitting on the sofa in her room, holding the weeping Mademoiselle Bourienne in her arms and gently stroking her hair. The princess's beautiful eyes, with all their former calm radiance, looked at Mademoiselle Bourienne's pretty face with tender affection and pity.
"No, Princess, I've lost your love forever!" said Mademoiselle Bourienne.
"Why? I love you more than ever," said Princess Mary, "and I will try to do everything I can for your happiness."
"But you must despise me. You, who are so pure, can never understand being swept away by passion. Oh, my poor mother..."
"I understand completely," Princess Mary answered with a sad smile. "Calm yourself, dear. I'll go to my father." And she went out.

Prince Vasili was sitting there with one leg thrown high over the other, a snuffbox in his hand, wearing a smile of deep emotion on his face, as if moved to his very core yet laughing at his own sentimentality. When Princess Mary entered, he hurriedly took a pinch of snuff.

"Ah, my dear, my dear!" he began, rising and taking both her hands. Then, sighing, he added: "My son's fate is in your hands. Decide, my dear, good, gentle Marie, whom I have always loved as a daughter!"
He stepped back, and a real tear appeared in his eye.

"Hmph... hmph..." Prince Bolkonsky snorted. "The prince here is making you a proposal on behalf of his pupil — I mean, his son. Do you or do you not wish to become the wife of Prince Anatole Kuragin? Answer: yes or no," he shouted, "and then I reserve the right to state my opinion as well. Yes, my opinion, and only my opinion," he added, turning to Prince Vasili in response to his imploring look. "Yes or no?"
"My wish is never to leave you, Father — never to separate my life from yours. I don't want to marry," she answered firmly, looking at Prince Vasili and then at her father with her beautiful eyes.

"Nonsense! Rubbish! Nonsense, nonsense, nonsense!" Prince Bolkonsky cried, frowning and seizing his daughter's hand. He didn't kiss it but simply pressed his forehead against hers and squeezed her hand so hard that she winced and let out a small cry.
Prince Vasili stood up.

"My dear, I must tell you that this is a moment I will never, never forget. But, my dear, won't you give us even a small hope of touching that kind and generous heart? Say 'perhaps'... The future is so long. Say 'perhaps.'"
"Prince, what I have said is everything in my heart. I thank you for the honor, but I will never be your son's wife."

"Well, that settles it, my dear fellow! I'm very glad to have seen you. Very glad! Go back to your rooms, Princess. Go!" said the old prince. "Very, very glad to have seen you," he repeated, embracing Prince Vasili.

"My calling is different," thought Princess Mary. "My calling is to find happiness of another kind — the happiness of love and self-sacrifice. Whatever it costs me, I will arrange poor Amelie's happiness. She loves him so passionately, and she repents so deeply. I will do everything I can to bring about their marriage. If he isn't rich, I'll give her the money. I'll ask my father and Andrew. I'll be so happy when she becomes his wife. She is so unfortunate — a stranger, alone, helpless! And, oh God, how passionately she must love him to have forgotten herself so completely! Perhaps I might have done the same!..." thought Princess Mary.
